The ADR template

On this page

Field notes — what we learned building a production agent ​

Every line below cost something to learn. They are grouped by the part of the system they shaped; the code cites them where it applies.

Models ​

  • A model cannot be told to be reliable. Instructions lower a slip rate; they never zero it. A model that filled a list "for the user" did so in 8 of 40 chats; the better model in 1 of 64 even with a note covering that case. The guard made it 0 for every model.
  • Models differ in where they slip. One rejects a fixed temperature, one needs a thought signature echoed back, one sends buttons with no prose on skills tuned for another. Configure each endpoint separately; never run a lowest-common-denominator setting.
  • Per-model notes belong to the endpoint, appended only when that model serves the call. One model's corrective notes are noise to another.
  • Prompt text is not free. Three review paragraphs raised one scenario's flake rate from 0 in 16 to 4 in 8. Measure a prompt change over several runs and compare failing sets.
  • Compare models on blended cost under YOUR prefix, not list price. With a ~40k-token cached prefix per call, the cache-read price and the cache-write surcharge decide the bill.
  • A model run-to-run varies a lot (32–45 of 45 on identical code in one day). Never judge a change on one run; compare the sets of failing scenarios over three.
  • Failover must happen before the first streamed token; afterwards a second endpoint would duplicate text. Keep the user's draft persisted so "try again" loses nothing.
  • Reasoning-model knobs change what tools are allowed. Some endpoints accept function tools only with reasoning effort "none" on chat completions. Put the knob on the endpoint.

Prompts and skills ​

  • One question per turn. Several questions in one message make the next reply unattributable; a bare value while several slots are open must be attributed explicitly.
  • Never combine an options question with free-text asks in the same turn.
  • Anything a record knows is shown and confirmed, never asked. The product moment is "we already know your unit"; letting it slide silently into the summary wastes it.
  • Any choice from reference data with ≥2 options is chips or a list, never prose. An irrelevant chip is the real bug, not a lone chip.
  • Say "never announce the step after it"; do not enumerate steps or give example phrases. Telling the model what the runtime does made it narrate "photos, video and visibility".
  • Describe the runtime's lines, never quote them. A model imitates lines it has seen in the history ("Taking this as Sale. Right?") and re-asks them.
  • Off-scope asks get "that's outside what I can do here", never "let's finish this first" — the latter implies it could be done later. Declare capabilities from the installed domains.
  • A tool parameter named like a UI heading invites a UI heading. header became "Choose at least 5 key features" and the reference lookup returned nothing.
  • Load only the in-play variant's skill and tools. 103k → 44k characters per call, the suite 30% faster, rate-limit waits gone. Once the type is set, remove it from the tool's enum or the model re-sets it "to be safe" (27 of 37 calls).

Reading what the user said ​

  • Read a reply by its WHOLE content, never its first word. 235 of 521 realistic messages were mis-read by a leading-word reader; 0 by the whole-content reader.
  • Widening the yes-vocabulary opens the next hole. Add only words that cannot carry content; rewrite look-alike hand-offs into non-yes tokens; keep the create gate strictest.
  • A lone number must be the whole message before it is a value ("make it 3 bathrooms" is not a price).
  • Explicit words win over inference (a stated purpose beats a figure's size); questions are not statements; a message cut off after a connector is never a bare yes.
  • A figure said with a money unit is not an id ("40 L a month" is not unit 40).
  • A confirm of the shown value plus a plain remark settles; a question, a "but", a second figure or a refusal does not.

Runtime-owned steps ​

  • Validate tools are stateless: the runtime's settle call must send the whole typed draft or the problems list lies.
  • A failed validate (an MCP error) must never read as a successful validate.
  • Carry settled values into every validate/preview/create call; a different value stands only when the user said it in words since.
  • The draft the pane shows is built from the arguments the MODEL passed, so guards run on those arguments in place, not on a copy.
  • Reset dependents on a change: price → the analytics verdict, furnishing → fixtures, type → specification, fewer photos → the video choice, project → everything below it.
  • A runtime-answered turn is stored with its blocks, so a reload draws it again; the transcript endpoint draws the open ask on the last entry.
  • A step waits for a complete draft; it never asks over an incomplete record.
  • Every runtime moment emits a behaviour event with counts and enums only, never text.
  • Runtime-answered turns must not count against the per-session rate limit: a user tapping through five cards in a minute is the product working (a prod chat hit the limit on its 11th tap).

The write path ​

  • Probe first. The first backend accepted a create with EVERY field stripped (0 rejections in ~90 cases); misspelled duplicate keys were the real schema; a "prod" base URL shared the dev database; a GET …/status/update/{id} wrote; a POST to an unknown admin route created a record. Never probe unknown routes with POST; treat any 200 with an id as a write.
  • The confirm gate ×3. The model attested confirmed:true after the user sent a change.
  • Timeout + idempotency on the write, keyed by session + draft fingerprint; reconcile an ambiguous failure before creating again.
  • No silent fuzzy fallback on the write path. Fuzzy matching is for suggestions; the write uses only ids the user confirmed.
  • An environment write guard must not be a substring test ("development" in the host name). Use an explicit flag that must equal the literal "true".
  • Whole-document PUT: read, change only allow-listed paths, re-read right before the write, write, read back, say one line. Compare references by id (a GET may populate them).
  • Create seeds its own status event when the server injects nothing — a record with an empty status history was invisible in every tab.

Clients ​

  • Upload ≠ attach. Files upload at once, keys wait on the session, attach the instant the write returns an id; the create payload ships an empty media block so a media hiccup never blocks the main write. Attach is idempotent. Bytes cross the MCP boundary as a temp file, never base64 over stdio.
  • A model-emitted link block is XSS in every host page without a scheme allowlist.
  • Fence junk is real: one block in forty came with junk glued to the closing fence, a two-backtick close, or no fence at all; the stream must hold back fence fragments.
  • A model re-emits its pre-tool text after the tool answers — dedupe sentences and blocks.
  • The user's bubble shows a readable echo of a form submit, not the wire text.
  • Pin the widget's script URL to its version; a proxy's cache can hide a shipped fix for hours.
  • "List another" = a new session; one chat = one job.
  • A completed chat's replay must not resurrect link pills the live turn filtered out.
  • Completion links are composed from today's templates, not the ones stored at create time.

Sessions and stores ​

  • A session id must not be a bearer credential; with an open listing endpoint it was a full hijack chain. Owner checks answer 404.
  • Any bearer string read any chat until identity was verified against the auth service. Verify, cache 60 s, fail closed.
  • Never load every persisted session into RAM at startup; hydrate on miss, evict idle.
  • A windowed history must never orphan a tool call from its result; both providers answer 400 forever.
  • node-redis reconnects forever: bound the first connect or startup hangs on a down Redis.
  • Any session-taking route that calls a tool must attach the request's bearer first; tokens are never persisted with sessions.
  • A process whose stdout is a protocol channel must log to stderr (the MCP child's info lines were silently parsed as JSON-RPC noise).
  • stdout is synchronous under Docker: log off the main thread.

Observability and cost ​

  • A feature is done when it is visible on a panel: a span, a counter or behaviour event, a log line with the trace id, a panel when someone will look.
  • OTLP/JSON failed on non-zero doubles with our backend; protobuf did not. Custom span attributes arrive as strings — cast in panel SQL. A field exists only after a span carried it, so always emit the attributes panels filter on, and prime counters at startup.
  • Search the telemetry for a private string after building a private path; a note typed by the user turned up in a span input and a trace line until redaction covered every carrier.
  • Users see a percentage of their cap, never tokens. Plan tokens (cost-weighted) track the bill with r = 1.00; raw totals varied 2.4×, billable-only 8.9×.
  • Bill what vendors bill you; a cache hit on your own infrastructure costs nothing.

Process ​

  • Evals before and after every change. When a check fails, decide out loud: check brittleness (fix the check) or a real regression (fix the agent) — and record which.
  • Classify every red: green on a serial rerun = model flake (ledger it); red on a clean baseline worktree too = pre-existing; else a regression. A credit outage mid-run is a transport error, not a result.
  • Shard the suite; 12 shards against a mock finish in minutes; 3 shards is the ceiling against a real provider's rate limit; 6 hit it.
  • Run the full gate, not a targeted subset: it caught two regressions the unit tests missed.
  • Mutation checks prove the checks bite: text mutants in scratch copies of the repo.
  • The eval runner's own copy of the rules goes stale: share the reader with the runtime.
  • Do not run the gateway while editing readers; it loads code at start.
  • One branch per fix; never push to a branch with an open PR. Three races with merges.
  • Never give hour-scale estimates unprompted; give the parallel number and what is cut.
  • Fix the class in code, not the instance; add an every-scenario check for it.
  • Don't ask for confirmation on small, obvious things inside the branch; ask for real decisions, pushes, flags that change what ships.
  • Unattended device work touches nothing private; credentials stay the owner's to type.
